source_text: Κἀγὼ οὖν προσδοκῶ ὑπό τινος τῶν ὠνομασμένων ἐπιβουλευθῆναι καὶ ξύλῳ ἐμπαγῆναι, ἢ κἂν ὑπὸ Κρίσκεντος τοῦ φιλοψόφου καὶ φιλοκόμπου. Οὐ γὰρ φιλόσοφον εἰπεῖν ἄξιον τὸν ἄνδρα, ὅς γε περὶ ἡμῶν ἃ μὴ ἐπίσταται δημοσίᾳ καταμαρτυρεῖ, ὡς ἀθέων καὶ ἀσεβῶν Χριστιανῶν ὄντων, πρὸς χάριν καὶ ἡδονὴν τῶν πολλῶν τῶν πεπλανημένων ταῦτα πράττων. Εἴτε γὰρ μὴ ἐντυχὼν τοῖς τοῦ Χριστοῦ διδάγμασι κατατρέχει ἡμῶν, παμπόνηρός ἐστι καὶ ἰδιωτῶν πολὺ χείρων, οἳ φυλάττονται πολλάκις περὶ ὧν οὐκ ἐπίστανται διαλέγεσθαι καὶ ψευδομαρτυρεῖν· ἢ εἰ ἐντυχών, μὴ συνῆκε τὸ ἐν αὐτοῖς μεγαλεῖον ἢ συνεὶς πρὸς τὸ μὴ ὑποπτευθῆναι τοιοῦτος ταῦτα ποιεῖ, πολὺ μᾶλλον ἀγεννὴς καὶ παμπόνηρος, ἰδιωτικῆς καὶ ἀλόγου δόξης καὶ φόβου ἐλάττων ὤν. Καὶ γὰρ προσθέντα με καὶ ἐρωτήσαντα αὐτὸν ἐρωτήσεις τινὰς τοιαύτας καὶ μαθεῖν καὶ ἐλέγξαι, ὅτι ἀληθῶς μηδὲν ἐπίσταται, εἰδέναι ὑμᾶς βούλομαι. Καὶ ὅτι ἀληθῆ λέγω, εἰ μὴ ἀνηνέχθησαν ὑμῖν αἱ κοινωνίαι τῶν λόγων, ἕτοιμος καὶ ἐφ᾿ ὑμῶν κοινωνεῖν τῶν ἐρωτήσεων πάλιν· βασιλικὸν δ᾿ ἂν καὶ τοῦτο ἔργον εἴη. Εἰ δὲ καὶ ἐγνώσθησαν ὑμῖν αἱ ἐρωτησεις μου καὶ αἱ ἐκείνου ἀποκρίσεις, φανερὸν ὑμῖν ἐστιν, ὅτι οὐδὲν τῶν ἡμετέρων ἐπίσταται· ἢ εἰ καὶ ἐπίσταται, διὰ τοὺς ἀκούοντας δὲ οὐ τολμᾷ λέγειν ὁμοίως Σωρκάτει, ὡς προέφην, οὐ φιλόσοφος ἀλλὰ φιλόδοξος ἀνὴρ δείκνυται, ὅς γε μηδὲ τὸ σωκρατικὸν ἀξιέραστον ὂν τιμᾷ· Ἀλλ᾿ οὔτι γε πρὸ τῆς ἀληθείας τιμητέος ἀνήρ“. Ἀδύνατον δὲ Κυνικῷ. ἀδιάφορον τὸ τέλος προθεμένῳ, τὸ ἀγαθὸν εἰδέναι πλὴν ἀδιαφορίας.
pass_a_gloss: And I therefore expect to be plotted against by one of the aforementioned and to be brought to a cross, or even by Crescens the lover of wisdom and lover of fame. For it is not worthy of a philosopher to say the man who publicly testifies against us about things he does not know, as if Christians are atheists and impious, doing these things for the sake of favor and pleasure of the many who have been deceived. For if, not having encountered the teachings of Christ, he reviles us, he is thoroughly wicked and much worse than private individuals, who often refrain from discussing and giving false testimony about things they do not know. Or if, having encountered them, he did not understand the greatness in them or, understanding, does such things in order not to be suspected, he is much more ignoble and thoroughly wicked, being less than private and irrational glory and fear. And for I added and asked him certain such questions and learned and refuted that he truly knows nothing, I want you to know. And that I speak the truth, if you have not been annoyed by the conversations of words, I am ready to converse with you again about the questions; and this would also be a royal work. But if my questions and his answers were known to you, it is clear to you that he knows none of our things; or if he does know, he does not dare to say so to those listening, similarly to Socrates, as I said before, he shows himself not to be a lover of wisdom but a lover of fame, who does not even honor the Socratic thing, which is worthy of honor. But no man is to be honored before the truth. And it is impossible for a Cynic, who has set indifference as his goal, to know the good apart from indifference.

pass_b_english: I therefore expect to be plotted against by one of those already named and brought to the cross, perhaps even by Crescens, the lover of wisdom and lover of fame. He is not worthy to be called a philosopher, for he publicly testifies against us concerning things he does not understand, charging that Christians are atheists and impious, and he does this for the favor and pleasure of the many who have been led astray. If he reviles us without having encountered the teachings of Christ, he is thoroughly wicked and far worse than private citizens, who often refrain from discussing or bearing false witness about things they do not know. But if he has encountered those teachings and failed to grasp their greatness, or if he grasped it yet acts in this way so as not to be suspected of allegiance, he is all the more ignoble and thoroughly wicked, subordinate to private, irrational glory and fear. I want you to know that I approached him, put certain questions to him, and discovered and demonstrated that he truly knows nothing. If the records of our conversations have not yet reached you, I am ready to share those questions with you again; that too would be a royal work. But if my questions and his answers have already become known to you, it is clear to you that he knows nothing of our doctrine; or if he does know, he does not dare say so to his hearers, any more than Socrates did, as I said before. He shows himself not a lover of wisdom but a lover of fame, one who does not even honor the Socratic principle that is worthy of honor: that no man is to be honored above the truth. And it is impossible for a Cynic, who has made indifference his goal, to know the good apart from indifference.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Greek text, including the distinction between the two possible motivations of Crescens (not encountering vs. encountering but not understanding/hiding his understanding). Pass B correctly renders 'τὸ σωκρατικὸν' as 'the Socratic principle' and 'ἀδιαφορίας' as 'indifference', maintaining the philosophical context. The translation of 'ἐμπάγηναι ξύλῳ' as 'brought to the cross' is standard and faithful.

The Greek text is correctly identified as Justin Martyr's Second Apology 8. The translation preserves the original meaning, including negation, agency, modality, and doctrine. Scripture is not cited in this passage. The title 'Expectation of Persecution' accurately reflects the content. All source paragraphs are accounted for. No uncertainties are present.
